finalProject.title: Rubric-Aware Agentic Proposal Builder with Human-in-the-Loop Critique and Verifiable Revision
finalProject.topic: An agentic, rubric-aware system that turns a rough research idea into a complete, citation-grounded research proposal through human-in-the-loop critique and a verifiable revision loop
finalProject.keywords: research proposal generation, agentic AI, rubric-aware evaluation, human-in-the-loop revision, citation grounding, verifiable LLM systems
finalProject.abstract: This project proposes an agentic, rubric-aware system that helps researchers transform a rough research idea into a complete, citation-grounded research proposal. The system decomposes proposal writing into specialized stages: requirement extraction, section planning, literature and source grounding, draft generation, rubric-based critique, human feedback incorporation, and verifiable revision. Unlike generic large language model writing assistants, the proposed system explicitly represents proposal requirements as a checklist and uses iterative critique loops to detect missing sections, unsupported claims, weak novelty statements, and evaluation gaps. A human-in-the-loop interface allows users to accept, reject, or modify agent suggestions while preserving an auditable revision history. The expected outcome is a prototype that improves proposal completeness, alignment with rubrics, citation traceability, and user efficiency compared with baseline LLM drafting workflows.
finalProject.problem:
CS students writing their first research proposal often struggle to translate a rough idea into a complete, rubric-compliant, citation-grounded proposal. TAs who review these proposals need to determine not only whether the final text is complete, but also whether claims are supported and whether revisions addressed critique findings. Generic LLM assistants can draft fluent text, but they often omit rubric requirements, hallucinate or weaken citations, and provide limited auditable revision support. This creates a need for a proposal-building workflow that supports novice researchers while giving reviewers a verifiable run log of requirements, evidence, critiques, user decisions, and revisions.
Domain/constraints: CS NLP course final project; single student; one quarter; LLM API with a local deterministic fallback
finalProject.novelty: Prior work and comparable tools include general-purpose LLM chat systems such as ChatGPT, one-shot proposal generators, retrieval-augmented writing assistants, and compliance-oriented tools such as Civio. These systems can help draft text or check broad requirements, but they typically do not treat a proposal rubric as an executable specification that drives generation, critique, and revision. This project is novel in combining rubric-grounded coverage checks, citation-grounded claim tracking, weak-claim detection, human-in-the-loop decision capture, and a measurable before/after revision loop. Each revision is linked to checklist items, source evidence, critique findings, and user decisions so that improvement in proposal quality can be verified rather than merely asserted.
finalProject.goal: The goal is to design, implement, and evaluate a prototype system that converts a rough research idea into a complete research proposal while improving rubric coverage, citation grounding, revision transparency, and user control compared with a single-pass LLM drafting baseline.
finalProject.method: Use intake, planning, retrieval, drafting, rubric critique, human decision, and revision agents operating over a structured JSON proposal state and audit log.
finalProject.figure: Show a pipeline from user idea and rubric to requirement extraction, planning, retrieval, drafting, critique, human decisions, revision, and final proposal, with feedback loops and an evidence store.
finalProject.expectedResults: Expected results include: (1) a working prototype that accepts a rough research idea and checklist and outputs a structured proposal; (2) a rubric-to-section mapping that shows which requirements are satisfied; (3) citation-grounded claims with source metadata or source notes; (4) an iterative critique and revision mechanism that improves proposal quality over multiple turns; and (5) an evaluation report comparing the system against baseline LLM drafting. Research milestones include requirements analysis, workflow design, prototype implementation, retrieval and citation grounding integration, rubric critic development, user interface development, evaluation, and final documentation.
finalProject.timeline: Estimated 12-week timeline: Weeks 1–2: define proposal rubric, target users, evaluation criteria, and baseline workflows. Weeks 3–4: design system architecture, JSON project state, agent roles, and prompt templates. Weeks 5–6: implement intake, planning, drafting, and structured output generation. Weeks 7–8: integrate retrieval, citation metadata, and claim-source linking. Weeks 9–10: implement rubric critique, revision loop, and human decision interface. Week 11: run evaluation using sample rough ideas and human or expert ratings. Week 12: analyze results, document limitations, prepare final proposal, prototype demo, and release plan.
finalProject.evaluation: Evaluate on 12 rough ideas across 3 domains. Metrics: required-section coverage (target 13/13), number of high-severity unsupported claims (target 0 after one revision), and a 1-5 human rubric score for novelty/method/evaluation (target mean >= 4). Compare draft v1 vs revised v2 (before/after) and against a single-shot ChatGPT baseline.
finalProject.risks: Key risks include hallucinated or weak citations, overreliance on LLM-generated claims, poor retrieval quality, excessive workflow complexity, user fatigue from too many questions, and difficulty evaluating proposal quality objectively. Mitigations include using retrieval-grounded generation, requiring source metadata for factual claims, flagging unsupported claims, limiting open-ended questions to high-value missing information, maintaining an auditable revision log, comparing against clear baselines, and using both automatic rubric checks and human ratings.
finalProject.resources: Required resources include access to an LLM API or open-source language model, a retrieval source such as Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex, arXiv, institutional databases, or a curated paper corpus, a vector database or document index, a web or notebook interface, structured JSON storage for project state, and evaluation participants or expert reviewers. The release plan should include a prototype demo, prompt and workflow templates, anonymized evaluation examples, documentation, and, where licensing allows, open-source code for the agent orchestration and rubric validation components.

v1.claim: The expected outcome is a prototype that improves proposal completeness, alignment with rubrics, citation traceability, and user efficiency compared with baseline LLM drafting workflows.
v1.issue: The draft states improvement before evaluation and includes user efficiency without a defined metric.
v1.fix: Frame as a hypothesis and define metrics such as required-section coverage, unsupported-claim count, citation-link presence, human rubric score, and optional time-on-task.

v1.claim: These systems can help draft text or check broad requirements, but they typically do not treat a proposal rubric as an executable specification that drives generation, critique, and revision.
v1.issue: The comparative claim is plausible but broad; it needs scoped comparison to named tools or a source note.
v1.fix: Limit the claim to observed behavior of generic chat, one-shot generators, and the uploaded Civio note, or add a systematic comparison table during evaluation.

v1.claim: so that improvement in proposal quality can be verified rather than merely asserted.
v1.issue: The phrase is rhetorically strong and does not specify what counts as verification.
v1.fix: Replace with measurable verification criteria: checklist delta, linked critique-resolution records, citation metadata presence, and blinded human rubric ratings.

v1.claim: using an LLM API with a local deterministic fallback
v1.issue: The fallback mechanism is underspecified; deterministic fallback cannot replace generation unless its scope is limited.
v1.fix: Specify that the fallback covers checklist parsing, JSON validation, LaTeX compilation checks, and audit-log consistency, not full generative drafting.
